note: Vol. I No. 45. The issue that carries the town's fire ordinance of 20 September 1834 whole and readable on page 4 — the FOUR WARDS with their boundaries, the four Fire Wardens by name, and a stove-pipe and chimney code that describes what Chicago houses were built and heated with. Beside it the earth-from-the-streets ordinance of 29 September. Page 3 carries the first printing of the notice that puts the Democrat's own office at the corner of Clark and South Water, John T. Temple's three-storey store house, and the month's best-placed shops: J. L. Wilson & Co. on Dearborn next door to the boot and shoe store, J. K. Botsford at the corner of Dearborn and Lake, and a stove store in Water-st. near the bridge. Page 3 also prints the 1 October post-office list for the first time, in the worst of its three states.

claims.notes: THE FOUR WARDS OF CHICAGO, DRAWN IN WORDS, AND THE FOUR MEN PUT IN CHARGE OF THEM. This is the most consequential claim of the October run and probably of the whole 1834 read so far, because it is a DOCUMENTED PARTITION OF THE TOWN with the boundary lines named: the first ward east of the centre of Lasalle street between Jackson and South Water; the second west of the centre of Lasalle between Jackson and East Water; the third everything north of the river; the fourth everything west of the north and south branches. Three of the four boundaries are streets this reconstruction already stands on the ground, and the fourth is the river itself — so a ward number, wherever one turns up later, is a POSITION. The wardens are named: William Worthingham, Edward E. Hunter, Ezekiel Resigue and James Kinzie. THIS IS THE BETTER OF TWO WITNESSES IN THE SAME MONTH: 1834-10-01 page 3 column 1 prints the same ordinance a week earlier with its left edge destroyed, where the first ward reads `Past of the centro of Lasalle` and `1 te dukson and South Water ts.` and the second ward's closing street is lost entirely. Reading them together is what settles that the second ward's limit is EAST Water street and not a repeat of South Water. THE WARDENS' NAMES CARRY THE WEAKEST OCR ON THE PAGE and they are recorded at exactly the strength the two printings support. `William Worthingham` is joined from this issue's `3 thingham` and 1834-10-01's `William Wor.`, which is a clean join. `Edward Hunter` is recorded WITHOUT a middle initial: this printing gives `Edwar.` and 1834-10-01 gives `Edward F. Hanter`, so one witness has no initial and the other reads it `F.`, and asserting either would be a choice rather than a reading. The third warden is recorded by SURNAME ALONE, `Resigue`: this printing gives `Eepael Resig` and 1834-10-01 gives `Sumnel Hhesigue`, forenames that cannot both be right, so neither is taken. `James Kinzie` is clean here and reads `Jere Kiteie` in the earlier printing, and this witness is preferred.

And be it Ordained as afor[esaid, That] it shall not be lawful for any person [or persons] to pass or cause to be passed, any st[ove pipe at]tached to any stove within the buildi[ng, through] the roof, wooden partition, la[t]h or [plaster part]ition of any house, store or building [within the] limits of the corporation of the Tow[n of Chica]go, unless said pipe be passed th[r]ou[gh a stone] or earthern cylinder, or be surround[ed by brick,] or be passed [th]ro[ugh] a tin or shee[t iron plate,] the inside of which shall not appr[oach or be] within one quarter of an inch of th[e pipe, nor] shall the pipe of any stove be nea[rer than … ] inches to any wood or other combu[stible matter;] and [e]very stove pipe or chimney pas[sing through the roo]f shall extend […] Inches of said [building… No] Pipe shall be passed [through the] side or end of any building within th[e limits of] the corporation.
claims.notes: WHAT A CHICAGO HOUSE WAS MADE OF, LEGISLATED. A building code from the autumn before the scene date, and it describes the fabric it is trying to stop burning: houses and stores with WOODEN PARTITIONS and LATH-AND-PLASTER partitions, heated by STOVES rather than fireplaces, with the stove pipe run out through the ROOF. What the ordinance permits is the detail a reconstruction can build: a pipe may pass through a stone or earthenware cylinder, or be surrounded by BRICK, or go through a TIN OR SHEET IRON PLATE held a quarter of an inch clear of the pipe; the pipe or stove must stand clear of woodwork; and a pipe may NOT be taken out through the side or the end of a building — only up through the roof. So the 1834 roofline carries pipes and not chimney stacks, and the plate around them is metal. The clearances themselves are the two numbers this witness loses: the inches to combustible matter and the inches a pipe must stand above the roof are both cut, and 1834-10-01's printing loses them too, so they are `[…]` here and not filled from anywhere.

claims.notes: THE INSPECTION, THE PRICE AND THE DATE. Every chimney and every stove pipe in the town is to be looked at on the FIRST MONDAY OF EVERY MONTH, offences reported, and anything dangerous pulled down at the owner's expense — which is a town whose officers walk into buildings once a month, and a fabric someone thought needed it. Five dollars an offence. The ordinance takes effect on 12 October 1834 and REPEALS an earlier fire ordinance of 6 November 1833, so Chicago had been legislating about fire since within a fortnight of the Democrat's own first issue. The clerk's signature is lost at the foot of the column and is not supplied; the president's is John H. Kinzie, as it is on the second ordinance of 1834-10-01 and on the fire-warden ordinance of 11 October (1834-10-22, claims c008 and c009).

claims.notes: PEOPLE WERE DIGGING THE STREETS UP, and the town had to forbid it. An ordinance of 29 September 1834 makes it unlawful to carry earth away from any street inside the corporation except by the supervisor of roads' order and for the purpose of repairing the street. Two things fall out of that for a reconstruction. First, an 1834 Chicago street is made of EARTH — loose enough to be worth a cartload, and mended with earth taken from somewhere else. Second, the town has a SUPERVISOR OF ROADS, an office this corpus had not met before. THIS WITNESS IS THE POORER OF THE TWO and the supplies are correspondingly heavy: 1834-10-01 page 3 column 1 prints the same ordinance with a cleaner middle (`remove or take`, `om off any of the etree`, `f the corporntion, unless`, `PRON of the sun`, `tom, and or te saPOrFINOF of roa`, `thie parpose of repairi`) and the two together are what make the supplies above readable at all. Every one of them is bracketed and none adds a fact neither witness carries.

claims.notes: A SECOND STOVE AND TIN DEALER, AND A PLACEMENT AGAINST THE BRIDGE — 'their store in Water-st., near the bridge.' The bridge is the drawbridge over the river's main stem, which the same month's `For Sale` of a two-storey building calls out directly ('nearly opposite the draw-bri[dge] … situated [o]n South Water-street', 1834-10-01 page 3 column 3), so this is a Water Street frontage close to the crossing. THE PROPRIETOR IS THE PART THIS CLAIM CANNOT CLOSE: the firm's name sits on the line above the quoted range in a block the OCR turned to `[uncertain: ONDE ? RENG,` and it is bracketed as a supply from 1834-10-15 page 3 column 2, where `PLOUGHS, for eale cheap by … JONES & KING` stands two inches away in the same standing set. That is a supply from ANOTHER ISSUE and is the weakest kind this run makes; the business is therefore recorded under the firm name with the reasoning stated here, and a reader who rejects the join still has the store, the street and the bridge.

claims.notes: THREE BUILDINGS IN ONE ADVERTISEMENT, ONE OF THEM WITH A HEIGHT AND A WHARF. A THREE-STOREY store house forty feet on one side with a WHARF ATTACHED OF SIXTY FEET; a small dwelling house of FIVE ROOMS; and a large store on SOUTH WATER STREET. A three-storey warehouse is the tallest structure this corpus has yet named in the town, and a sixty-foot wharf in front of it is a river frontage with a length. It belongs to John T. Temple, whose house on Lake Street is the anchor G. Blanshard advertises against in the same month (1834-10-22, claim c004). THIS WITNESS IS THE POOREST OF THREE and is cut down its left edge (`ARGE thi te Store House, 40`); the storeys and the wharf are supplied from the two later printings, which are unambiguous — 1834-10-15 page 3 column 4 reads `ARGE three story Stoyg House, 40 by 27` with `Sicet, with a wharf atta@hed, of 60 fect` under it, and 1834-10-22 page 3 column 4 reads `GE three stury Store House, 49 by` and `et, with a wharf attached, of G8 feet`. claims.notes: A BOOKSELLER AND STATIONER OPENS IN A NAMED MAN'S BUILDING ON WATER STREET. This is a third kind of placement — not a corner, not a neighbour, but a LANDLORD'S BUILDING, 'P. B. Carpenter's', which for a reconstruction is a frontage that has to be somebody's before it can be this shop's. THE READING IS THE WORST OF THE MONTH and the claim is kept deliberately thin because of it: the partners' names are half destroyed (`hesow Bassi, of Boston` gives a Boston man whose forename may be Jason and whose surname may be Bassett, and the second partner is lost entirely), so NO PERSON IS MINTED from this claim at all. What survives and is worth keeping is the trade, the building and the street. A later pass with the page images should be able to close the names; nothing here guesses them.

claims.normalized: […] JOHN S. C. HOGAN, P. M.
claims.notes: THE SAME 1 OCTOBER LETTER LIST, IN ITS FIRST PRINTING — this is its foot, and the head is at the top of the previous column (`in the Post Office at [Chicago]`, page 3 column 1). It is recorded here as a NOTICE and not as persons, because in this issue the segmenter's crop loses the list's left-hand sub-column almost entirely: nearly every row of the A-to-H names survives as two or three letters. The list is extracted at name level from the printing of 1834-10-22 instead, where both sub-columns of the second half read clean (claims c001 and c002 there), and no name is minted twice. What this claim carries is the fact of the insertion and its date, which is what makes three printings of one list countable.
